prompt: Run this as a fresh Python script. The three next calls in print are evaluated from left to right. Which option gives the complete stdout line and a correct account of cursor ownership? items is a built-in list; no mutation occurs.

snippets.code:
items = [10, 20, 30]
cursor = iter(items)
alias = iter(cursor)
fresh = iter(items)
print(next(cursor), next(alias), next(fresh))

options.text: 10 10 10. iter(cursor) creates an independent cursor starting at the beginning, just like iter(items).
options.feedback: An iterator's iter operation returns that same iterator, not a fresh traversal. cursor and alias therefore share progress: their successive next calls yield 10 and 20. Only fresh starts independently at 10.

options.text: 10 20 30. Every iterator over items shares one position stored on the list, so all three next calls advance that position.
options.feedback: The list does not own a single shared traversal position. Separate iter(items) calls create independent cursors. cursor and alias are one iterator, but fresh is another and still yields 10 on its first next.

options.text: 10 20 10. iter(cursor) returns cursor itself, while the second iter(items) creates an independent iterator over the same original list.
options.feedback: Correct. The first next advances the cursor shared by cursor and alias; their two calls yield 10 then 20. fresh has independent progress and its first call yields 10. Independent cursors do not require copied source lists.

options.text: 20 30 20. A new iterator already points at the first item, so next moves ahead before reading and skips that item.
options.feedback: A new list iterator's first next returns the first item, not the second. Applying that to the shared cursor and the independent fresh iterator gives 10 20 10.

options.text: 10 20 10. cursor and alias share one cursor and fresh has another because every iter(items) first copies the whole source list into a private snapshot.
options.feedback: The line and cursor sharing are right, but source copying is not. These built-in list iterators retain cursors over the original list. Separate iteration positions do not imply separate copies of that list.
options.partial_reason: Correct: all three printed values, shared progress for cursor/alias, and independent progress for fresh. Incorrect: claims iter(items) implicitly copies the entire source list into a private snapshot rather than iterating the original list.

explanation: iter(items) creates a list iterator with its own position. Calling iter on that iterator returns the same iterator, so alias and cursor advance one shared position and yield 10, then 20. A second iter(items) creates another iterator whose position is independent, so fresh still yields 10. Both iterators refer to the original list; creating an iterator does not implicitly copy its source.

verification.rationale: The exact displayed script checks progress shared through an iterator alias versus an independent traversal of the iterable. With an unmodified source, a false private-snapshot model predicts the same line, so no-source-copy semantics require separate review.
verification.limitations: Built-in lists and their ordinary iterators only, not arbitrary custom iterable implementations. This is a cursor-ownership bridge rather than generator growth, laziness or exception-lifecycle behavior. One output cannot prove all protocol or source-identity claims, half-credit quality or calibration.
